title: The Doorway Rule. Why Every Screen Habit Should Have a Threshold
body: The machine I am writing on can do everything. That is its genius and, measured over the last decade, its trap. The same rectangle is my workshop, my bank, my newsroom, my arcade, and my mailbox, and it follows me to every room, so every room contains all of those at once. The experiment of the last month gave the rooms back their borders. I call it the doorway rule, and this is the measured report. The rule in one sentence. Every place gets one conversation with the machine. At the work desk, the machine may open work things. In the kitchen, recipes and messages to actual humans. In the bedroom, nothing; the bedroom's allotment is zero. No app was deleted, no blocker installed, no willpower mobilized beyond a question asked at each threshold. What room is this, and what is the machine allowed to be here? The whole system is a doorway and a pause, which is to say it costs nothing and cannot be upgraded, which is why it works. The findings, kept honestly. The work room changed first and most. Feeds, which had been colonizing the desk in stolen forty-second sips, one per gap in concentration, moved to the kitchen where they belong, and the desk's afternoon acquired a continuity I had forgotten from the era of separate machines. A task that used to take an interrupted hour now takes an uninterrupted forty minutes, and the twenty-minute saving is real but less interesting than the texture of the hour. Work with no drip. The kitchen, given feeds legally, stopped being a place of guilty scrolling, because guilt requires a violation and no violation is now possible; the feed in the kitchen is a chosen activity with a bowl of food, not a trespass in a room where I owed somebody my attention. The bedroom allotment of zero produced the month's hardest days and its largest return. The first four nights, my hands kept performing the reach to the nightstand that fifteen years had trained, and found nothing, and the boredom that followed was so acute it was practically informative. I had been ending every day with a digest of everyone else's emergencies. By week two the reach had extinguished and sleep came the old way, by darkness and fatigue. The phone now charges in the hallway, equidistant from all rooms and loyal to none, like a good referee. The failures deserve their paragraph, because a report without them is marketing. Twice I broke the rule with full awareness, once to answer a genuine emergency and once from pure appetite, and the second break reproduced the old drip for the rest of that evening, which is the most useful data point of the month. The rule is not a wall, it is a dam, and a dam with one deliberate hole is just a stream. And there was one real cost. Being unreachable in the bedroom means being unreachable in the bedroom, including by the one person whose 2 a.m. message I would always want. The compromise took two days to find. The ringer, never the screen, may follow me to bed. The transferable claim is about thresholds in general. Habits do not attach to intentions; they attach to places. Every place you let the machine be everything is a place where nothing can be itself. Assign the conversations. Let the desk be work, the kitchen be bread and gossip, the bedroom be nothing at all. The rectangle will resist for exactly four days. Then the rooms will take their borders back, and you will discover the border was never lost, only unlabeled.
